stops.name: Giza, the Battle of the Pyramids
stops.campa: Within sight of the pyramids of Giza the army forms its divisions into hollow squares, artillery and baggage sheltered within the ranks, to receive the charge of Murad Bey's Mamluk cavalry: the most magnificent horsemen Bonaparte's soldiers have ever faced, in cloth of gold, sabres flashing, each rider a small treasury of arms. The squares hold; disciplined volley fire breaks charge after charge, and the Mamluks are driven into the Nile or the desert. Legend will put in the general's mouth, gesturing at the monuments across the river, the sentence that outlives the battle's true tactics by far.
stops.quote: Soldiers, from the summit of these pyramids, forty centuries look down upon you.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bonaparte before the battle, first printed by Gourgaud in 1823, likely a later legend rather than words spoken on the field

stops.name: Cairo, the founding of the Institut d'Égypte
stops.campa: In a requisitioned Cairo palace Bonaparte founds the Institut d'Égypte on the model of the Institut de France, and takes his own seat not as commander but as an ordinary member, under the presidency of the mathematician Monge. Berthollet, the naturalist Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, the artist Denon, and a hundred and fifty savants measure the Sphinx and survey the temples of Karnak and Luxor, founding the modern study of ancient Egypt in the months before Nelson's fleet, one August night, burns the transport ships at anchor in Aboukir Bay and seals the army inside the country it has just begun to read.

stops.name: Acre, the failed siege
stops.campa: Before the walls of Ottoman Acre, defended by the Turkish governor and the British commodore Sidney Smith with guns taken from Bonaparte's own captured siege train, the march north out of Egypt breaks. Two months of failed assault, plague among the wounded, and no breach; Bonaparte visits the pest-house himself, they say, and touches the dying to steady his men. He lifts the siege and marches the wreck of the army back across the desert to Egypt, his first campaign ended in outright failure, and confides to his staff the empire of the East he might have built had this one town fallen.
stops.quote: If I had been able to take Acre, I would have put on a turban... I would have made myself emperor of the East, and I would have returned to Paris by way of Constantinople.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recorded conversation on Saint Helena

stops.name: Fréjus, the return to France
stops.campa: Abandoning the army he commands to Kléber without leave of the Directory that sent him, Bonaparte slips past the British blockade in two frigates and lands at Fréjus to a welcome no defeated general fleeing his own war should expect: church bells, crowds unhitching his carriage horses to draw it themselves, bonfires along the road to Paris. The Republic he finds on his return is bankrupt, invaded on every frontier, and ruled by a Directory that has burned through its credit with the nation. Egypt already forgotten, all France seems to be waiting only to be told what to do next, and by whom.

stops.name: Saint-Cloud, the 18 Brumaire
stops.campa: Moved on a pretext to the palace of Saint-Cloud, away from the Paris mob, the two legislative councils meet under the guard of Bonaparte's own soldiers. In the Orangerie the deputies of the Five Hundred, sensing the trap, mob him physically, tear his coat, and shout him outlaw; he is white and shaking when his brother Lucien, president of the council, saves the coup by declaring falsely that deputies had drawn daggers on the general. Murat's grenadiers clear the hall at bayonet-point, and by night three Consuls rule France in place of five Directors. The Revolution, Bonaparte tells the nation, is over.
stops.quote: Citizens, the Revolution is fixed upon the principles which began it. It is ended.
stops.quote_source: Bonaparte's proclamation of 19 Brumaire, Year VIII (10 November 1799)

stops.name: Marengo, lost at five, won at seven
stops.campa: Surprised by the Austrian army of Melas near the farmhouses of Marengo, the First Consul's forward divisions are driven back all morning, and by five in the afternoon the battle looks lost, the field littered with French dead and stragglers streaming to the rear. Then General Desaix's division, recalled at a gallop, strikes the disordered Austrian columns in the flank; Desaix falls dead in the first charge, and Bonaparte, shown the body that evening, is seen to weep, and forbidden, by the mask of command he must wear, to weep as he wishes. The rout becomes a French victory that saves the Consulate before it is a year old.
stops.quote: I lost the battle at five o'clock; I won it back again at seven.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recollection of Marengo (widely cited period attribution)

stops.name: Paris, the Code civil promulgated
stops.campa: After four years of drafting sessions the First Consul himself has chaired, arguing points of inheritance and contract with the jurists Portalis, Tronchet and Cambacérès late into the night, the Code civil des Français is promulgated in a single text of over two thousand articles: civil equality, secular marriage, careers open to talent, property secured, feudal privilege abolished for good. It will be carried by his armies into a dozen countries and outlast every one of his crowns. Long after Saint Helena he will say this, not Austerlitz, is the work that will not be washed away.
stops.quote: My true glory is not to have won forty battles... Waterloo will erase the memory of so many victories. But what nothing will erase, what will live eternally, is my Civil Code.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, recorded on Saint Helena (widely cited memoir attribution)

stops.name: Paris, Notre-Dame, the self-coronation
stops.campa: In Notre-Dame, before Pope Pius VII and the assembled dignitaries of the new Empire, Napoleon has the crown of Charlemagne carried to the altar, and at the moment the pontiff would set it on his head he turns, takes the crown from the tray himself, and places it on his own head before crowning the kneeling Joséphine beside him. The gesture is calculated to the inch: no priest, no king gives him this; he takes it, and Rome merely attends. Outside, cannon salute for hours and Paris roars for the new Emperor: acclaim that a young Venezuelan named Bolívar, watching from the crowd, will remember longer than the crown itself.
stops.quote: Joseph, if our father could see us now!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to his brother Joseph during the coronation, 2 December 1804 (recounted in period memoirs)

stops.name: Milan, the Iron Crown
stops.campa: In the Duomo of Milan, six months after Notre-Dame, Bonaparte crowns himself a second time: King of Italy now, with the ancient Iron Crown of the Lombard kings, said to be forged from a nail of the True Cross. He lifts it from the altar himself, as at Paris, and sets it on his own head before the assembled notables of the new kingdom, pronouncing the old Lombard warning aloud. Days later, at the grand review on the plain outside the city, a young traveler from Caracas named Bolívar watches the Emperor ride past within arm's reach amid the blaze of his marshals, and studies the little man in grey the way a rival studies a rival.
stops.quote: God gives it to me; beware whoever touches it.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon at his coronation as King of Italy, Milan, 26 May 1805 (the traditional Lombard formula, per period accounts)

stops.name: Austerlitz, the sun
stops.campa: On the first anniversary of his coronation, on the frozen Pratzen heights near the little Moravian town of Austerlitz, Napoleon lures the combined armies of Austria and Russia, the two emperors watching from the field themselves, into abandoning the high ground, then strikes the weakened center with Soult's divisions out of the morning mist as, famously, the sun breaks through. Sixteen thousand Allied dead and prisoners against under nine thousand French; the Third Coalition is broken in a single day. His soldiers will remember 'the sun of Austerlitz' for the rest of their lives as the luckiest light that ever rose on them.
stops.quote: Soldiers, I am pleased with you... it will be enough for you to say, 'I was at the battle of Austerlitz,' for people to reply, 'There is a brave man.'
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's proclamation to the army after Austerlitz, 3 December 1805

stops.name: Jena-Auerstedt, Prussia broken in a day
stops.campa: On a single October day the two wings of the Grande Armée shatter the army of Frederick the Great's heirs at Jena and at Auerstedt twelve miles apart: Napoleon commanding the larger action without even realizing, until evening, that Davout's single corps has alone destroyed the main Prussian army at Auerstedt while the Emperor merely mopped up a secondary force at Jena. Fortresses that held Frederick's cannon surrender without firing a shot; the King and Queen of Prussia flee to the Russian frontier. On the very plateau where the philosopher Fichte had once lectured on the free self, the old Prussian state ceases, for years, to exist as more than a name on French maps.

stops.name: Bayonne, the Spanish Bourbons abdicate
stops.campa: At the château of Marracq outside Bayonne, having lured both Spanish claimants across the frontier under promise of arbitration, Napoleon extracts the crown from father and son in three days: on the fifth of May Charles IV renounces the throne to him outright; that same day, not yet knowing of his father's act, Ferdinand VII abdicates in Charles's favor, unwittingly signing the crown straight through to the French Emperor. Napoleon hands Spain, a nation he has never troubled to understand, to his brother Joseph within the week: the single act, more than any battle, that teaches all Europe the word guerrilla and opens the wound that never fully closes.
